evidence_quotes.quote: Theoretical access to drinking water is 61%, falling below 20% in informal neighborhoods.
A total of 655 households were sampled in 67 blocks for the survey.
Poor regular connection to the drinking water network has been recorded in areas where most households lack formal land titles.

Surveys indicate that 29.74% of households have not established land titles for their plots. The main reasons cited are inheritance of the land, the cost of the procedures, and administrative burdens.
Among tenants, surveys report frequent disagreements over the payment of water bills, leading in some cases to the temporary disconnection of homes when bills are not paid.
In informal settlements, the lack of a land registry, irregular plot sizes, and complex occupancy statuses make it difficult to secure the right-of-way necessary for installing pipes.

criterion_notes.c1: Examines household and neighborhood drinking water service access in Bukavu, DR Congo, including public network connection (REGIDESO), public standpipes, unimproved sources, and parallel water markets.
criterion_notes.c2: Satisfies BOTH the plain wording and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism reading, though borderline in framing because physical urban sprawl and topography are the headline exposures. Under the plain wording, the study clearly examines urban governance, historical urban planning frameworks (1927-2021), institutional fragmentation, and land tenure governance. Under the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading, the study goes beyond unanalysed macro-governance background by collecting primary household survey and institutional interview data on specific rule-type mechanisms governing water access: (1) land tenure/documentation status and administrative burden (29.74% of surveyed households lack formal land titles due to inheritance, procedural costs, and administrative burdens, and 4.03% hold conflicting parallel titles from overlapping customary, administrative, and informal tenure regimes, with poor regular water network connection concentrated where households lack formal titles); (2) cadastral and right-of-way rules preventing REGIDESO from securing legal/operational right-of-way to install pipes in untitled informal settlements; (3) unsystematic building permit/title issuance and weak enforcement of urban planning standards; and (4) cost-recovery/disconnection enforcement among tenants experiencing temporary home disconnection when water bills go unpaid.
criterion_notes.c3: Mixed-methods primary empirical study combining a structured survey of 655 households across 67 blocks in all 14 districts of Bukavu, semi-structured interviews using six interview guides with REGIDESO officials and municipal/state technical services, archival analysis of urban planning documents, and multi-temporal GIS/remote sensing analysis (1980-2024).
criterion_notes.c4: Reports household drinking water access and connection rates (61% theoretical citywide access, <20% in peripheral/informal neighborhoods, 45%-75% across communes), main water source shares (45% public standpipes, 32.8% unimproved sources, 43.7% parallel market), distribution frequency (3-6 days/week), collection distance and average collection time (45 min), water prices, and temporary disconnections for bill non-payment.
criterion_notes.c5: Population and unit of analysis (655 surveyed households across 67 blocks/14 districts/3 communes in Bukavu, plus neighborhood spatial strata and utility/municipal actors), exposures (urban sprawl, informal settlement/lack of formal land titles, administrative burdens in titling, lack of cadastral right-of-way, non-enforcement of planning/building permits, and bill-payment disputes), outcomes (network connection/access, source reliance, collection time/distance, price, temporary disconnection, waterborne disease), and study design (cross-sectional mixed-methods survey/interview study with diachronic GIS analysis) are all clearly identifiable. While inferential statistics focus on spatial distance, time, price, and disease rather than a regression effect estimate for land titling, quantitative synthesis eligibility (Criterion 6 in INCLUSION_EXCLUSION.md) is not a systematic-review inclusion gate.
criterion_notes.c6: Full text is written in English.

study_design: Cross-sectional mixed-methods case study combining a structured household survey, semi-structured key-informant interviews, archival planning analysis, and diachronic GIS/remote sensing spatial analysis (1980-2024)
population_and_sample: Households in Bukavu, South Kivu Province (n = 655 surveyed households across 67 blocks in 14 districts and 3 communes: Bagira, Ibanda, and Kadutu), alongside neighborhood/municipal spatial units and key informants from REGIDESO and municipal/state technical services
exposure: Uncontrolled urban sprawl and informal settlement expansion interacting with land tenure insecurity and lack of formal land titles (overlapping customary, administrative, and informal tenure systems; procedural costs and administrative burdens of titling; parallel land titles; lack of cadastral right-of-way for utility pipes), unsystematic building permit and urban planning enforcement, and tenant water-bill payment disputes
outcome: Household drinking water access and REGIDESO network connection coverage, reliance on public standpipes, unimproved sources, and the parallel water market, distribution frequency (days/week), collection distance and time, water prices, temporary disconnection for non-payment, and waterborne disease occurrence
rationale: This 27-page mixed-methods empirical study (household survey n = 655, semi-structured institutional interviews, archival planning review, and multi-temporal GIS analysis) examines drinking water service access in Bukavu, DR Congo, satisfying all systematic-review inclusion criteria (c1-c6). Although the overarching framing centers on urban sprawl and steep-slope geomorphology, Section 3.3, Section 3.4, and Section 4.3 empirically examine concrete rule-type legal and administrative mechanisms governing drinking water access under the 2026-10-13 Criterion 2 clarification: household lack of formal land titles (29.74%, attributed in the survey to inheritance, procedural costs, and administrative burdens) and parallel titles (4.03%) under overlapping customary/administrative/informal tenure regimes, cadastral and occupancy barriers preventing REGIDESO from securing pipe rights-of-way in informal settlements, unsystematic building-permit/title issuance and weak enforcement of urban planning standards, and temporary disconnections among tenants due to unpaid water bills. Because qualitative and descriptive empirical mechanism evidence is eligible for the systematic review even without a dedicated regression effect size on the legal exposure, the record is included with medium confidence.
